issues.subcategory: Significance claim contradicts reported p-value
issues.description: The discussion states the meta-analytic effect size for Connect was 'significantly different from zero,' but the results section clearly reports p = .065, which is not statistically significant at the conventional α = .05 level. This mischaracterization directly affects the interpretation of whether the original finding for perceived opportunities to connect with others was replicated.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: Sample sizes below stated minimum
issues.description: The methods state that all studies 'collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study),' but Table 1 shows that four of the seven studies had sample sizes below 120: BYU-Sp16 (N=90), BYU-Wi17 (N=90), Gordon (N=80), and SAU (N=81). This directly contradicts the stated inclusion criterion and raises questions about how quality checks were applied.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.subcategory: FSN value for Express contradicts between sections
issues.description: The results section reports the fail-safe number (FSN) for Express Self as 3 studies, but the discussion section claims 'only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant.' These numbers are inconsistent, and the discrepancy undermines confidence in which value is correct.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies.

issues.subcategory: FSN value for Connect contradicts between sections
issues.description: The results section reports the FSN for Connect as 5 studies, while the discussion reports it as 11 studies. One of these values must be incorrect, and the difference (5 vs. 11) is substantively meaningful when evaluating the robustness of the finding.
issues.quote: The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.subcategory: Prediction interval and confidence interval swapped in Discussion
issues.description: For Self-Disclosure Safety, the results section reports the 95% CI as [-.40, -.15] and the 95% PI as [-.54, -.03]. However, the discussion reports the PI as [-.40, -.15], which is actually the CI from the results section. The PI is the wider interval [-.54, -.03]. This matters because the PI is the appropriate interval for predicting future study results, and reporting the narrower CI as the PI overstates precision.
issues.quote: The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy between original Advantageous beta and effect size r
issues.description: Table 1 reports the original study's standardized beta for Advantageous as -.300, while Table 3 reports the original effect size r as -.33. The note to Table 1 states 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient,' but these values differ. For bivariate regression, β should equal r. This discrepancy suggests either the original study included additional predictors (making r a partial correlation), or there is a calculation error. If the original used multiple regression, comparing partial correlations from the original with zero-order correlations from the replications introduces a systematic comparability problem.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: Original Advantageous effect size differs between abstract and tables
issues.description: The abstract reports the original effect size for Advantages as -.30 (matching the beta in Table 1), while Table 3 and the discussion report it as -.33. This inconsistency, combined with the beta/r discrepancy, creates confusion about which value is the correct original effect size for comparison.
issues.quote: self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)

issues.subcategory: Equivalence of r and beta assumed without justification
issues.description: The note to Table 1 asserts that 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient,' which is only true for bivariate (simple) regression with a single predictor. If the original Forest and Wood (2012) study included covariates or multiple predictors, the t-statistics and df reported would yield semi-partial or partial correlations, not zero-order correlations. The observed discrepancy for the Advantageous outcome (β = -.30 vs. r = -.33) provides evidence that this assumption may be violated for the original study, potentially making the original and replication effect sizes non-comparable.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of CI and PI for Express Self
issues.description: The results state that 'the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14,' implying both intervals are identical. While this is mathematically possible when estimated between-study variance is zero, it should be explicitly explained. As written, it is ambiguous whether two intervals coincidentally overlap or whether the authors are reporting only one interval.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent scoring across replication studies
issues.description: The authors note that the Gordon study appeared to sum rather than mean-average items, while other studies used mean averaging. Although standardized regression coefficients should be invariant to linear transformations, this introduces uncertainty about data quality and consistency. Additionally, the descriptive statistics reported in Table 2 would not be comparable across studies, potentially complicating interpretation.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: RSE response scale variation
issues.description: Two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a 5-point RSE scale instead of the original 4-point scale. Changing the number of response options can alter distributional properties (e.g., skewness, kurtosis), reliability, and mean-level responses. While standardized coefficients partially mitigate this, the change constitutes a deviation from the direct replication protocol that could affect comparability.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale

issues.subcategory: Underpowered studies for smaller effects
issues.description: The original Connect effect size was r = -.22. At α = .05 (two-tailed), detecting this effect with 80% power requires approximately N = 160. Most replication studies (N = 80–116) were underpowered for this effect. Even the CREP-specified minimum of N = 120 provides only ~60% power for r = .22. The MSU study (N = 374) is adequately powered, but the majority are not, limiting the informativeness of individual significance tests for the smaller effects.
issues.quote: Sample sizes ranged from 80 to 374.

issues.subcategory: No assessment of Facebook usage status
issues.description: Neither the original study nor the replications appear to screen or control for whether participants actively use Facebook. Participants who rarely or never use Facebook would have different (and arguably less valid) perceptions of its affordances for self-disclosure, expression, and connection. This is especially relevant given that the replications were conducted 4–5 years after the original, during which Facebook usage among college students declined relative to Instagram and Snapchat.
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012)

issues.subcategory: Incomplete CREP project completion rate not analyzed
issues.description: Only 7 of 17 teams that started the replication process completed and posted data. The 59% non-completion rate is not analyzed for potential selection bias. If teams that found null or unexpected results were less likely to complete (file-drawer at the team level), the included studies may not be representative. This is a form of selective attrition that could bias the meta-analytic estimates.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 'forks' representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository.

issues.subcategory: Insufficient publication bias assessment
issues.description: The authors rely solely on fail-safe number (FSN) analysis to assess publication bias, which is widely regarded as a weak and potentially misleading test (e.g., Becker, 2005). More informative methods such as funnel plots, Egger's regression test, PET-PEESE, or p-curve analysis were not conducted. Given that the paper invokes publication bias in the original study as an explanation for effect size differences, a more rigorous assessment is warranted.
issues.quote: we conducted a fail-safe number (FSN) analysis (Rosenberg, 2005) using the fsn function. The FSN analysis was intended to identify the number of non-significant, unreported studies required to add to the meta-analysis to reduce a significant meta-analytic result to non-significance.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete documentation of data handling procedures
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives about missing data handling, composite score calculations, or data exclusions. Without this information, it is impossible to evaluate whether data preprocessing was consistent across sites or to replicate the meta-analysis from raw data. This is particularly concerning given the known inconsistencies in scoring (sum vs. mean) and scale differences.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: Missing data handling not described
issues.description: The manuscript provides no information about how missing data were handled at the individual study or meta-analytic level. Were participants with missing items excluded listwise? Were items pro-rated? Given that surveys were administered in different formats (online vs. in-lab) and some studies had smaller samples, missing data rates and handling could meaningfully affect results.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling

issues.subcategory: Temporal changes in social media landscape
issues.description: The original study was likely conducted circa 2010-2011, while the replications were conducted in 2016-2017. During this period, Facebook's dominance among college-aged users declined substantially in favor of Instagram and Snapchat. The authors acknowledge this in the discussion but do not account for it in the analysis design (e.g., by measuring or controlling for social media platform preferences). This temporal confound is arguably the most important alternative explanation for differences between original and replication findings.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others, whereas these platforms would not have been a consideration for participants in Forest and Wood's (2012) study.

issues.subcategory: Abstract omits significant meta-analytic result for Express
issues.description: The abstract states that 'self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% CIs for effect sizes included zero),' but omits that the meta-analytic effect was statistically significant (r = .08, p = .021). While individual study CIs did include zero, the combined estimate was significant. Selective reporting in the abstract could mislead readers about the nature of the findings.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero)

issues.subcategory: Procedural variations across replications not tested as moderators
issues.description: Known procedural differences include: in-lab vs. online administration, individual vs. group testing (SAU ran groups of 2-6), RSE item wording/order differences (IIT-Sp16), 4-point vs. 5-point RSE scale, and inclusion of additional measures in Direct-Plus replications. None of these were formally tested as moderators. While the small number of studies (k=7) limits moderator analyses, the authors could have examined whether specific procedural deviations tracked with outlier effect sizes (e.g., BYU-Sp16 showing opposite-direction effects for Safety).
issues.quote: Because each of these potential moderating factors occurred in only one or two of the seven replications, we chose not to explore these issues in more depth.

issues.subcategory: Overstatement of support for Advantageous finding in summary
issues.description: The summary states researchers can be 'relatively confident of finding that low self-esteem predicts perceptions that Facebook is a safer and more advantageous place to self-disclose.' However, the Advantageous finding was described as 'mixed' throughout the results and discussion: only 4/7 replications found significant effects, the meta-analytic effect (-.16) was about half the original (-.33), and three studies showed non-significant effects. The summary treats Safety and Advantageous as equally well-supported, which overstates the evidence for Advantageous.
issues.quote: future researchers can be relatively confident of finding that low self-esteem predicts perceptions that Facebook is a safer and more advantageous place to self-disclose than FTF interactions

issues.subcategory: Predictive language implies directionality from cross-sectional data
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, self-esteem is described as 'predicting' Facebook perceptions, using language that implies a directional relationship. All studies employed cross-sectional, correlational designs. While regression is being used for prediction in the statistical sense, phrases like 'low self-esteem predicts perceptions' can be misread as implying that self-esteem causally determines these perceptions. The reverse direction (Facebook perceptions influencing self-esteem) or third-variable explanations are not discussed.
issues.quote: individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions

issues.subcategory: Demographic information inconsistently collected
issues.description: Race data were collected in only 3 of 7 replications, and the original study's demographic reporting was incomplete (6% 'undisclosed' gender). The lack of consistent demographic data prevents examination of sample composition differences as potential moderators and limits assessment of generalizability. Age distributions also varied widely (mean ages 19.3 to 26.2, SDs 1.4 to 9.7), suggesting meaningfully different populations.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneity CI interpretation limitations not noted in results
issues.description: The 95% CIs for I² are extremely wide in several analyses (e.g., Express: [0%, 79%]; Connect: [0%, 91.69%]; Advantages: [0%, 79.94%]). The authors acknowledge in the limitations that heterogeneity estimates are biased with small numbers of studies, but in the results section, conclusions about heterogeneity are stated without this caveat (e.g., 'did not appear to be heterogeneous' for Express when the CI upper bound is 79%).
issues.quote: The between-study variance in the replication studies did not appear to be heterogenous, Q(df = 6) = 4.75, p = .576; T2 = 0, 95% CI [0, .03]; I2 = 0%, 95% CI [0%, 79%].

issues.subcategory: Item wording differences in one replication
issues.description: The IIT-Sp16 study had 'slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items' on the RSE. Changing wording on 40% of the scale items is a non-trivial deviation for a direct replication. This study also showed among the largest effect sizes for Safety (-.445) and Connect (.160), raising questions about whether these differences affected measurement properties.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all')
